title: Reading anti-Muslim bias in the news

targeted_hostility.label: Hostility directed at Muslims
targeted_hostility.definition: Identify evidenced threatening, abusive, or hostile expression targeting people because they are Muslim or perceived to be Muslim.

stereotyping_and_intent.label: Stereotyping intended to encourage hatred
stereotyping_and_intent.definition: Assess stereotyping intended to encourage hatred of Muslims. If intent is not established by context, explicitly mark insufficient_context rather than claiming it.

discrimination_claim.label: Reports or statements of unequal treatment
discrimination_claim.definition: Identify stated exclusion or unequal treatment directed at Muslims; do not pronounce legal unlawfulness from a passage.

racialization.label: Treating Muslims as a single suspect group
racialization.definition: Assess treating Muslims or perceived Muslims as a homogeneous, inferior, threatening, or inherently suspect population.

exclusion.label: Exclusion linked to Muslim identity
exclusion.definition: Identify expressed exclusion, discriminatory expectations, or restrictions attached to Muslim identity.

institutional_pattern.label: Possible repeated institutional practice
institutional_pattern.definition: Identify an evidenced institutional practice or repeated pattern. One passage cannot by itself establish a systemic pattern; mark insufficient context when required.

cases.heading: Whose stereotype is this?
cases.reading: A jewellery advertisement showed an interfaith family. The article attributes the accusation to activists and calls it a conspiracy theory. That wording matters when interpreting the flag.
cases.followup: Check who made the allegation and how the reporter introduced it. Assigning the activists’ claim to the journalist would reverse the reading.

ref.text: Indian right-wing activists claimed the commercial promoted “love jihad,” a conspiracy theory whereby Muslim men are accused of converting Hindu women to their faith by marriage.
ref.quote: Indian right-wing activists claimed the commercial promoted “love jihad,” a conspiracy theory whereby Muslim men are accused of converting Hindu women to their faith by marriage.

cases.context: Indian right-wing activists claimed the commercial promoted “love jihad,” a conspiracy theory whereby Muslim men are accused of converting Hindu women to their faith by marriage.
cases.criterion: Treating Muslims as a single suspect group
cases.explanation: Right-wing activists used the 'love jihad' conspiracy theory to characterize Muslim men as inherently predatory in marriage.

cases.heading: One school decision, two different questions
cases.reading: The account identifies a concrete condition for attending class. The next paragraph reports that lower courts backed the principal and that the Supreme Court later affirmed the student’s right to wear the hijab.
cases.followup: A case can support a reading of unequal treatment. Establishing a repeated practice would require records from other cases, dates or schools.

ref.text: An example of such is the famous 2016 case of the Somalia student who wore hijab to class, and was pressured by the school's principal to take off her headscarf or face expulsion.
ref.quote: An example of such is the famous 2016 case of the Somalia student who wore hijab to class, and was pressured by the school's principal to take off her headscarf or face expulsion.

cases.context: An example of such is the famous 2016 case of the Somalia student who wore hijab to class, and was pressured by the school's principal to take off her headscarf or face expulsion. The principal received support from Islamophobic movements and political parties, and was even awarded a medal in 2018 by the right-wing Czech president Zeman for being “a brave woman in the fight against intolerant ideology, for services to the state”.
cases.criterion: Reports or statements of unequal treatment
cases.explanation: The text reports a case where a student faced potential expulsion for wearing a hijab, with initial court decisions supporting the principal's pressure.

cases.heading: What does the author actually support?
cases.reading: The final paragraph calls for freedom to choose whether to wear a veil. The model marked the author as supporting the proposition about the risk of discrimination.
cases.followup: Read the proposition alongside the stance. Support for a woman’s freedom of choice gives this author-attributed flag a very different meaning from support for discrimination.

ref.text: It is not about a woman covering her face or not, but about whether she will be able to live without being judged and discriminated against.
ref.quote: It is not about a woman covering her face or not, but about whether she will be able to live without being judged and discriminated against.

cases.context: The challenge today is to protect individual freedom without turning it into another form of dominance. Governments must stop using secularism or religion as tools for social engineering. It is not about a woman covering her face or not, but about whether she will be able to live without being judged and discriminated against.
cases.criterion: Reports or statements of unequal treatment
cases.explanation: The author highlights the risk of women being judged and discriminated against based on whether they cover their faces.

cases.heading: A flag to challenge
cases.reading: The sentence identifies women as the group barred from care. Neither this sentence nor its paragraph gives Muslim identity as the basis for the restriction. That basis is required by the exclusion criterion.
cases.followup: A reviewer should ask what evidence connects this restriction to religious identity. The published count includes the original flag and keeps this challenge alongside it.

ref.text: Under the first Taliban regime, women were barred from accessing medical care.
ref.quote: Under the first Taliban regime, women were barred from accessing medical care.

cases.context: Afghanistan’s women’s health system has long reflected the country’s political instability. Under the first Taliban regime, women were barred from accessing medical care. The U.S.-backed era brought clinics and training — but only as long as foreign aid lasted. Many professionals have since fled.
cases.explanation: The text describes systemic restrictions on women's rights and professional participation under the Taliban regime, including being barred from medical care and facing interrogation for interacting with male colleagues.

cases.heading: A possible miss in an unflagged article
cases.reading: The paragraph identifies the Uyghurs as a Muslim Turkic people, then reports labels applied to them in Chinese mainstream media. The model recorded that the group-stereotyping criterion was unmet in this unit.
cases.followup: A reviewer should examine whether these reported labels construct the group as inherently suspect and how ethnic and religious targeting intersect. The article attributes the labels to the media.

ref.quote: Widely portrayed as “motherland separatists” or simply “terrorists” in Chinese mainstream media, this group has been targeted more systematically since Xi Jinping became president of China in 2012.

cases.context: There are 11 million Uyghurs, a Muslim Turkic nation, living in the western province of Xinjiang in China. Widely portrayed as “motherland separatists” or simply “terrorists” in Chinese mainstream media, this group has been targeted more systematically since Xi Jinping became president of China in 2012.
cases.origin: Sentence selected by the editor from software-attached unit references
cases.criterion: Treating Muslims as a single suspect group

cases.heading: A religious reference can be biographical
cases.reading: The article lists milestones in Samia Suluhu Hassan’s presidency. Her religious identity is part of the biographical description. The cited sentence describes no threat or abuse.
cases.followup: The word Muslim brought this article into the sample. A reader still needs a target and hostile expression to support a targeted-hostility flag.
